proposal.title: Trump Sues Federal Officials Over Tribal Casino Licensing
proposal.description_short: In a lawsuit reported May 4, 1993, Trump challenged federal tribal-casino licensing rules and argued they favored tribal operators.
proposal.description_medium: An Associated Press report published by the Los Angeles Times on May 4, 1993, described a civil lawsuit by Donald Trump, his organization, and his three Atlantic City casinos against federal officials over tribal gaming. The complaint challenged treatment under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act. Trump’s attorney said the suit sought state authority to accept or reject tribal gambling operations rather than a blanket prohibition. These arguments are claims made by the plaintiffs, not judicial findings.
proposal.description_long: An Associated Press report published by the Los Angeles Times on May 4, 1993, described Donald Trump’s federal lawsuit challenging the treatment of tribal casinos under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act of 1988. The named defendants included Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt and the chairman of the National Indian Gaming Commission. The plaintiffs were reported to include Trump, his organization, and three Atlantic City casinos. The complaint argued that tribal operators received preferential treatment in casino licensing and that the federal statute intruded on states’ powers to regulate and tax gambling within their borders. Attorney John Barry told the reporter that the plaintiffs were not seeking a complete ban on tribal gambling; he described a request for states to have greater authority to approve or reject operations. Those legal contentions are the plaintiffs’ assertions, not findings that the statute was discriminatory or unconstitutional. The reviewed report does not establish the exact complaint filing day or the lawsuit’s ultimate disposition. Accordingly, the entry uses the May 4 publication date and does not claim that a court adopted Trump’s legal position.
